source.title: Steering Knowledge Selection Behaviours in LLMs via SAE-Based Representation Engineering
source.authors: Yu Zhao; Alessio Devoto; Giwon Hong; Xiaotang Du; Aryo Pradipta Gema; Hongru Wang; Xuan-Li He; Kam-Fai Wong; Pasquale Minervini

record.tranche_reason: The study reports that reconstructing edited activations from SAE codes caused accuracy to become nearly zero, bearing on whether SAE-feature-based steering can lose behaviour when the original activation is not retained. It does not directly measure dark matter as defined in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper's knowledge-conflict steering results and probing results do not measure SAE reconstruction error or the dark-matter properties in the claim, so they are not included as rows. The paper does report one relevant reconstruction-based result in Section 4.3. It gives no random-error comparison of equal size.
record.test_reason: This is a steering method paper (SpARE) that uses pre-trained SAEs as a tool and reports its own method's knowledge-selection accuracy against baselines. Its only contact with dark matter is one design-justification sentence in Section 4.3. That sentence says decoding an edited SAE code instead of keeping h causes information loss due to reconstruction loss and 'nearly zero accuracy'. No model, number, baseline or unedited-reconstruction control is given, and the effect is confounded with the edit itself. The paper builds its method on keeping the residual (adding decoded deltas to h), i.e. it assumes the error matters rather than measuring it. This is too thin to count as a test of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase describes a design detail, not the paper's conclusion. The authors conclude that knowledge conflicts are detectable by probing mid-layer residual streams. They propose SpARE, a training-free SAE-based editing method that steers use of contextual vs parametric knowledge, beating representation engineering (+10%), contrastive decoding (+15%) and ICL baselines on NQSwap and Macnoise. Steering works best at mid-layers, and the residual stream is more skewed when the model uses context. As a design choice they edit h additively rather than replacing it with SAE reconstructions, citing reconstruction loss and near-zero accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE features to steer knowledge selection and does not investigate the original study's dark-matter measurements or SAE reconstruction-error structure.
record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The relevant reconstruction result is qualitative and aggregate: the paper does not identify the models or conditions behind it, provide an uncertainty estimate, or compare with random errors of the same size.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's separately reported knowledge-selection steering scores, probing results, and layer analyses are not results about SAE reconstruction error or the claim's dark-matter properties.

untested.parts: No linear prediction of SAE error from activations.
No error-norm scaling across SAE sizes or per-token comparison.
No comparison of reconstruction loss against equal-norm random errors.
No split of the error into linear and nonlinear parts.
There is no quantified measurement of behaviour lost when the SAE error is dropped versus kept. The only evidence is an anecdotal statement about edited-code reconstruction.
SAE types differ (TopK, ReLU, JumpReLU), but no comparison of error magnitude or structure across training choices.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'supports' label for V5 is dropped. The study does not measure how much behaviour depends on the SAE error term; it asserts in passing that decoding edited codes breaks accuracy. Researchers may read Section 4.3 as weak anecdotal consistency with V5, but it gives no numbers, models or control separating reconstruction error from editing effects.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of SAE error is linearly predictable from input activations.
Error-norm scaling across SAE sizes, whether larger and smaller SAEs fail on the same tokens, and whether error persists with scale.
No comparison with random errors of the same size or reported model-loss comparison.
No separation of linear and nonlinear error components or test of their interpretations.

The result concerns reconstruction-based activation editing in the reported experiments; it does not quantify the share of behaviour lost generally, test circuits, or compare against equal-sized random errors.
No comparison of SAE training objectives, shrinkage, dead latents, architectures, or end-to-end training as explanations for dark matter.

rows.subject: Models in the S PARE experiments (not individually specified for this result)
rows.operation_detail: Reconstructed edited hidden states from SAE activations instead of retaining the original hidden state.
rows.note: The authors attribute the result to information loss from SAE reconstruction. They report it only in aggregate as occurring in their experiments, without specifying models or giving a comparison to random errors.
rows.check: The subject (models) is unstated, there is no numeric value or baseline, and no unedited-reconstruction control. The drop cannot be separated from the effect of the edit z' = z - z- + z+. It is a parenthetical design justification, not a reported experiment, so 'observed' overstates it.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SAE reconstruction-based activation editing in the reported experiments
reader_labels.reason: The paper states that reconstructing edited activations from SAE codes led to nearly zero accuracy, consistent with the importance of retaining information not captured by the SAE representation (r1).
